blocks.text: A compiler can accept a program that computes the wrong answer. A test can pass because it never exercised the boundary that matters. A pointer can contain a nonzero address after the object it once referred to has ceased to exist. Learning C++ begins with syntax, but it becomes useful when syntax is connected to contracts, object lifetime, evidence, and responsibility.

For C++, that means distinguishing source from executable, a value from its representation, an owner from a borrow, and a program’s exit status from proof that its application contract is satisfied.

topics.title: Audience and progression
topics.summary: No previous C++ experience is assumed. You should be comfortable creating files, opening a terminal or development environment, and following a directory path. Chapter 2 establishes the compiler and build tools. Concepts appear in a deliberate order: ordinary values and control flow precede containers; containers precede detailed pointer and manual-allocation reasoning; those foundations precede classes and the multi-file capstone.

blocks.text: The common source baseline is C++20. Most of Book I uses an intentionally smaller subset. A few names, such as std::string_view, std::move, and deleted copy operations, appear where they clarify a local example. Their immediate meaning is explained without claiming that the entire modern-language topic has already been covered. Book II develops resource safety, copy and move semantics, templates, ranges, and the broader standard library.

topics.title: Read for a decision, then trace the mechanism
topics.summary: Before running a program, state what question it answers. A compiler warning identifies a potential code issue; a runtime check compares an actual result with an expectation; a sanitizer observes certain executed defects. None of those tools replaces the other two. The useful habit is selecting evidence that addresses the specific claim you intend to make.

topics.title: Use failures deliberately
topics.summary: Intentional compiler errors and unsafe conceptual counterexamples belong in disposable scratch copies. They are not part of the default passing build. Never execute undefined behavior merely to see which answer it produces and then treat that observation as a language guarantee. Many important defects can be explained with an ownership or range argument before executing them.
